doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Balancing music with flying and the discipline of focus
summary: Piltzecker says he flies for the Coast Guard Auxiliary and that the focus it requires carries over to music.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: That’s an interesting question. I think I get pretty intensely interested in various things and go at them for a while and then sometimes they become a little bit more on the back burner and I try to bring whatever I do to some level of competence that I — never get satisfied but some level of competence that’s acceptable. So yes, I still love flying and I flew here and it’s a habit I — it’s really difficult to kick. It’s very intoxicating. It’s visual, it’s visceral, and it’s time when you have to think at a level that you don’t think all the time. I mean when you’re on final approach, you know, your mind is working a little bit differently than it works in normal life. You’re concentrating and more focused. And I love that, it’s just really fun. So that’s another thing about flying I love. That’s — I didn’t come here to talk about flying but yes, it’s part of me and I’m still very involved with it and I fly for the U.S. Coast Guard Auxiliary, I volunteer my time, so I do a lot of Coast Guard missions. But yeah, I’m very pleased to be able to sort of wrap that into the rest of my life.

Yeah. Do you have to make sure you’re not getting distracted by some recent composition that you’re working on, and all of a sudden your mind starts going there, and meanwhile you’re flying an airplane?

Well one discipline helps the other. You always learn something from this endeavor or activity like it’s applicable to something else. So the idea of focusing, when you’re doing solos, when you’re flying, the idea of having to not — consciously not be distracted, which we train to do, and so you can do the task, it helps sometimes on the bandstand. For instance, when you’re — you know I fly with a lot of guys who have various experiences, most of them are older than me, and you know we may not be of the same political persuasions let’s say, and it’s a very divided, polarized country right now, as we know. But the time not to engage in those conversations, if you can call them conversations, is not in the cockpit, because it’s distracting to the point where it’s

dangerous. So that’s a discipline you learn simply not to do that. And if it happens it’s a liability, a real serious liability. So you don’t talk about certain things by design, and you discipline yourself not to do that. So that kind of discipline sometimes can help your focus in other realms. Does that make sense to you?
